cafe.question: Ingredient costs jumped. What should I change?
cafe.page_title: Cafe cost decision — three choices compared
cafe.headline: Ingredient costs are up {shock}%. What should you do?
cafe.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your cafe and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
cafe.what_changed: Your suppliers put ingredient prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus simplifying the menu

cafe.unknown_why: Everything here turns on how many customers you lose when the price goes up. Nobody knows that number for your cafe — the figure used comes from research on eating out as a whole.
cafe.unknown_how: Raise the price of a few items for two weeks and count the orders. Two weeks of your own till data beats any research figure we can offer.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, or your competitors are raising prices too.
sens_help.central: The typical response found in research on eating out.
sens_help.high: Stress case: competitors hold their prices and customers have easy alternatives.

cafe.c_card_note: Depends on how much simplifying the menu cuts ingredient cost (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with the removed items ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your cafe.
cafe.chart_lede: Costs take about a week to rise — you are still using stock bought at the old price. Customers take a couple of weeks to react to a new price.
cafe.sources_note: Research gives a reference range for eating out as a whole. Your own customers may be more or less price-sensitive than that.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model the wider economy, seasons or new customers.

shop.question: My supplier raised prices. Should I pass it on?
shop.page_title: Shop cost decision — three choices compared
shop.headline: Your supplier put prices up {shock}%. Should you pass it on?
shop.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your shop and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
shop.what_changed: Your supplier put wholesale prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 4% rise plus dropping low-margin lines

shop.unknown_why: A shop's customers can often buy the same item elsewhere, so a price rise costs more orders here than in a trade where people come for you specifically. How much more is the thing nobody has measured for your shop.
shop.unknown_how: Put prices up on a handful of lines for two weeks and watch what happens to those lines against the rest. Your own numbers from the last time you raised prices work too.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, an awkward shop to replace, or competitors raising prices too.
sens_help.central: Our judgement: customers who could shop elsewhere, with some effort.
sens_help.high: The research figure for customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere.

shop.c_card_note: Depends on how much dropping low-margin lines cuts your cost of goods (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with those lines ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your shop.
shop.chart_lede: Costs take about three weeks to rise — the stock on your shelves was bought at the old price. Customers react to a new price within a week or two.
shop.sources_note: The research quoted measures customers switching between brands on the same shelf, which is easier than switching shops. It sets the top of the range rather than the middle.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model competitors, marketplaces or search ranking.

salon.question: My schedule is filling up. Is it time to raise prices?
salon.page_title: Salon pricing decision — three choices compared
salon.headline: Your diary is {shock}% busier. Is it time to raise prices?
salon.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your salon and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
salon.what_changed: Demand for appointments is up {shock}%, and your diary has a ceiling.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 5% rise plus shifting the mix

salon.unknown_why: There is no published figure for how salon clients respond to a price rise — not a weak one, none we could use honestly. Every setting on this control is our judgement, so your own test is worth more here than in any other trade.
salon.unknown_how: Raise the price of one service, or for new clients only, and count rebookings over six weeks.

sens_help.low: A loyal client base who book with you personally.
sens_help.central: Our judgement for an appointment business with real switching costs.
sens_help.high: Stress case: clients who treat it as a commodity and shop on price.

salon.capacity_note: Your diary has a ceiling, so some of the {unit} a price rise costs you were being turned away anyway. That is why raising prices costs less here than the price sensitivity alone suggests.
salon.c_card_note: Depends on how much shifting the mix cuts your cost per appointment (about {red} points here), how much it lifts the average ticket, and how many {unit} leave with the discounts ({loss}%). None is measured from your salon.
salon.chart_lede: Clients on a six-week cycle only meet a new price at their next visit, so the reaction arrives over a couple of weeks rather than at once.
salon.sources_note: We found no published figure for personal-care services that could be used honestly. Every setting on the price control is our judgement. The retail studies listed are only the reference points our range was positioned against.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual clients will behave.
Model hiring, longer hours or a second chair.
Model competitors, word of mouth or reputation.
